definition: A way for one server's network card to read or write another server's memory directly, without involving either CPU. It cuts latency and CPU load and is the basis of InfiniBand and RoCE GPU networking.
RDMA carried over ordinary Ethernet. It lets Ethernet fabrics do what InfiniBand does, but traditionally needed careful tuning to avoid packet loss and congestion collapse.
NVIDIA's name for a network card built for GPU-to-GPU traffic (ConnectX-8, ConnectX-9): high bandwidth per GPU plus on-card congestion control and packet reordering that cooperate with the switch.

An industry group (AMD, Broadcom, Arista, Cisco, hyperscalers and others) that published an open Ethernet transport for AI and HPC (UEC 1.0, June 2025; 1.1, October 2026) with multipath packet spraying and new congestion control.

Optical engines mounted in the same package as the switch chip instead of in pluggable modules at the front panel. Shorter electrical paths save power (vendors claim 3.5-5x) but make lasers and repairs harder to service.
Building optical components (modulators, waveguides, detectors) on silicon wafers with chip-making tools, so light-based links can be made in volume and placed next to electronic chips.
The number of ports on one switch chip at a given speed (e.g. 512 x 200G on a 102.4 Tb/s chip). Higher radix means fewer network tiers, fewer optics and fewer hops for the same number of GPUs.

A layered switch network (leaf, spine, core) in which every tier has as much bandwidth as the one below, so any GPU can talk to any other at full speed. A two-tier fat tree of radix-R switches connects up to R squared / 2 endpoints.
The delay of the slowest messages (e.g. the 99th percentile), not the average. In synchronous AI training every GPU waits for the slowest transfer, so the tail sets the step time.
The rules by which senders slow down when a link or switch queue fills up. Good congestion control keeps queues short and avoids dropped packets without leaving bandwidth idle.
Sending packets of one flow over several paths according to real-time load instead of a fixed hash. It evens out traffic but delivers packets out of order, so the receiving NIC must reorder them.
Spreading the packets of one message across all available network paths. Used by UEC, AWS SRD and Spectrum-X to avoid hot spots; requires out-of-order delivery support at the endpoint.
The circuit at the edge of a chip that turns parallel data into a high-speed serial signal on one wire pair and back. Lane rates (100G, 200G, next 400G) set port speeds for switches, NICs and NVLink.
A pluggable module that converts electrical signals to light and back at each end of a fiber link. AI clusters use several per GPU; makers include Innolight, Eoptolink and Coherent.

The digital signal processor inside a pluggable transceiver that cleans up and retimes the high-speed signal. Supplied mainly by Marvell and Broadcom; removing it (linear optics) saves power at the cost of reach.

A copper cable with retimer chips in its connectors that extend reach to several metres at 100-200G per lane, cheaper and lower-power than optics for in-rack and adjacent-rack links. Credo is the leading supplier.
A switch that steers light beams with tiny mirrors to reconnect fibers without converting to electrical signals. Google uses OCS in place of spine switches in Jupiter and in TPU pods.
AWS's network interface for HPC and AI instances, built on its Nitro hardware and the SRD protocol, which sprays packets over many paths and tolerates out-of-order delivery.

A switch chip with large packet memory (often HBM), such as Broadcom Jericho or Cisco P200, that can absorb bursts over long links. Used for scale-across between data centers and for scheduled AI fabrics.
A switch built by an ODM (e.g. Celestica, Accton) on merchant silicon, sold without a vendor operating system; the buyer runs SONiC, FBOSS or its own software.
The software that runs a switch: routing, telemetry, configuration. Examples are Arista EOS, Cisco NX-OS, NVIDIA Cumulus Linux and the open-source SONiC.
How much of one product a customer buys alongside another, e.g. dollars of networking per dollar of GPUs. A rising attach rate means a vendor captures more of each cluster's budget.
Mellanox/NVIDIA's Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol: the switch adds up gradients as they pass through, roughly halving the data each GPU must send in an all-reduce.
Wall-clock time to finish a training job or step. Network vendors quote JCT gains because they capture both bandwidth and tail-latency effects.
